content.title: A bug that took days
content.prompt: Tell a story about a difficult bug you solved.
guiding_questions: What did everyone believe the cause was at first?
What was the moment you realized you were wrong?
What did the fix actually change?
What would you tell your past self?

content.title: The outage
content.prompt: Tell a story about a production outage from the inside: what you saw, felt and did.
guiding_questions: Where were you when it started?
What was the point of highest tension?
What decision turned it around?
How did it end for the customers?

content.title: Teaching a concept
content.prompt: Tell a story about explaining a technical concept to someone and watching it click.
guiding_questions: What did they misunderstand before?
What analogy or moment changed it?
What could they do after?

content.title: The rewrite
content.prompt: Tell a story about a rewrite or migration, and what it cost.
guiding_questions: What is the one-line hook?
Where did the plan meet reality?
What is the lesson you actually believe now?

content.title: Disagreement I lost
content.prompt: Tell a story about a time you disagreed with someone and turned out to be wrong.
guiding_questions: What was at stake?
How did you argue your side?
How did you find out you were wrong?
What did you do about it?

content.title: First week at a new job
content.prompt: Tell a story about your first week at a job that surprised you.
guiding_questions: What did you expect?
What was the surprise?
How did it change how you worked?

content.title: Saying no
content.prompt: Tell a story about a time you said no to a customer, a manager or a colleague, and what happened.
guiding_questions: Why was yes the easy answer?
How did you say no?
What was the cost, and was it worth it?

content.title: Mentor
content.prompt: Tell a story about someone who changed how you work, in one specific moment.
guiding_questions: What were you like before?
What exactly did they say or do?
What is different now?

content.title: Unexpected problem
content.prompt: Tell a story about a time you had to solve an unexpected problem with no time to prepare.
guiding_questions: What was the plan before it broke?
What was the moment of decision?
How did it end?

content.title: Something that changed your perspective
content.prompt: Tell a story about something that changed your perspective.
guiding_questions: What did you believe before?
What was the event?
What do you do differently now?

content.title: A place
content.prompt: Tell a story set in a place that matters to you, so the listener can see it.
guiding_questions: What are the three sensory details?
What happened there?
Why does it matter?

content.title: Learning English
content.prompt: Tell a story about a moment when language got in your way, and what you did.
guiding_questions: What were you trying to say?
What went wrong?
How did you recover, and what changed after?

content.title: Boring event, interesting story
content.prompt: Tell a story that makes a boring event interesting: a commute, a meeting, a grocery run.
guiding_questions: What is the unexpected angle?
Where is the tension in something trivial?
What is the punchline or twist?

content.title: Embarrassing moment
content.prompt: Tell a story about an embarrassing professional moment that you can laugh at now.
guiding_questions: Build the setup calmly.
What is the exact moment it went wrong?
How do you land it with grace?

content.title: Failing at something
content.prompt: Tell a story about failing at something that mattered to you.
guiding_questions: What did you want?
What did you do?
What was the result, honestly?
What did the failure give you?

content.title: A hard conversation
content.prompt: Tell a story about a hard conversation you had to have with someone on your team.
guiding_questions: What was the situation, without blame?
What did you say first?
What did they say that you did not expect?
How was it resolved?

content.title: Taking ownership
content.prompt: Tell a story about taking ownership of something nobody asked you to own.
guiding_questions: Why was it unowned?
What did you do first?
What was the measurable result?

content.title: Origin story
content.prompt: Tell the origin story of a product or company you would start, as if to an investor.
guiding_questions: What is the moment you noticed the problem?
Who is the hero of the story: you or the customer?
What is the insight?

content.title: Customer who churned
content.prompt: Tell a story about a customer you lost and what it taught you.
guiding_questions: What did you assume about them?
What actually happened?
What changed in the product or the process?

content.title: Interview: proudest project
content.prompt: Tell me about the project you are proudest of.
guiding_questions: Situation in two sentences.
Your specific role and action.
The result, with a number if you can.

content.title: Interview: conflict
content.prompt: Tell me about a conflict with a colleague and how you handled it.
guiding_questions: Keep the other person human.
What did you do, not the team?
What was the outcome for the relationship?

content.title: The last server
content.prompt: Fictional: tell the story of the last on-call engineer on Earth, on the night the servers go quiet.
guiding_questions: Establish the world in two sentences.
What is the tension?
What is the choice at the climax?

content.title: The pitch that went wrong
content.prompt: Fictional: a founder pitches to an investor who is secretly their former CTO. Tell it.
guiding_questions: What is the hook line?
When does the recognition happen?
What is the lesson, played straight or for laughs?

content.title: Will AI reduce the number of software developers?
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: Will AI reduce the number of software developers? Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What has AI changed about your own development workflow in the last year?
discussion_points: What juniors used to learn by doing slowly
Whether engineering becomes easier or just different
Which skills gain value: judgment, taste, systems thinking
follow_up_questions: What will junior developers struggle with that you did not?
Will software engineering become easier?
What skills will become more valuable?
Are developers becoming overly dependent on AI?
What happens in five years?
content.controversial_angle: Isn't 'AI is just a tool' what every profession said right before it shrank?
content.closing_question: If you were 22 today, would you still become a software engineer?

content.title: What makes a great CTO?
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: What makes a great CTO? Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What is the job of a CTO, really, at a 30-person company versus a 300-person company?
discussion_points: Technical debt as a business conversation
follow_up_questions: What is the most common way CTOs fail?
How much should a CTO code?
How do you know when to hire a VP of Engineering?
What do you say to a CEO who wants everything faster?
content.controversial_angle: Most first-time CTOs are just the best engineer with a title. Is the role even real at seed stage?
content.closing_question: What would you tell yourself the day before you became a CTO?

content.title: Flutter in 2026: still the right bet?
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: Flutter in 2026: still the right bet? Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: Why did you choose Flutter in the first place?
discussion_points: React Native and Kotlin Multiplatform as alternatives
follow_up_questions: What kind of app should never be built in Flutter?
How has the ecosystem matured?
What do you tell a founder who wants iOS and Android in three months?
What is Flutter's biggest risk?
content.controversial_angle: Google kills products. Why should anyone bet a company on Flutter?
content.closing_question: What would make you switch away from Flutter?

content.title: Remote work, five years on
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: Remote work, five years on. Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What did remote work get right, and what did it quietly break?
follow_up_questions: How do you mentor someone you have never met in person?
What does a great remote engineering culture look like day to day?
Are return-to-office mandates about productivity or control?
What would you change about your own remote setup?
content.controversial_angle: Remote work is a senior-engineer privilege paid for by juniors who never learn. Agree?
content.closing_question: Fully remote, hybrid or office: what would you choose for a company you founded tomorrow?

content.title: Interviewing is broken
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: Interviewing is broken. Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What is the worst interview you have ever been on either side of?
follow_up_questions: What would your ideal process look like?
How do you evaluate judgment rather than memorization?
How should candidates prepare?
Has AI made cheating unavoidable?
content.controversial_angle: If interviews barely predict performance, why not hire on a two-week paid trial and fire fast?
content.closing_question: What is one question you always ask?

content.title: From engineer to founder
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: From engineer to founder. Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What did you have to unlearn as an engineer when you started selling?
follow_up_questions: What surprised you most about customers?
How do you split time between product and sales?
What is your biggest mistake so far?
What should a technical founder never delegate?
content.controversial_angle: Engineers make terrible founders because they fall in love with the solution. Convince me otherwise.
content.closing_question: What would you build if you could not write code?

content.title: Learning in your thirties
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: Learning in your thirties. Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: What are you deliberately learning right now, and how?
discussion_points: Active recall and speaking before reading
follow_up_questions: What is your system for not forgetting?
How do you learn something you find boring?
What did you get wrong about learning in your twenties?
content.controversial_angle: Most self-improvement is procrastination with better branding. Prove me wrong.
content.closing_question: What will you have learned by this time next year?

content.title: The monolith strikes back
content.prompt: You are the guest on a podcast. Episode: The monolith strikes back. Speak as if answering the host.
content.opening_question: Why are companies consolidating services back into monoliths?
follow_up_questions: Where did microservices genuinely pay off?
How do you keep a monolith modular?
What is the first sign you should split?
How do you migrate back without a rewrite?
content.controversial_angle: Microservices were a hiring strategy dressed up as architecture. Agree?
content.closing_question: What architecture would you pick for a new startup today, and why?

vocabulary.meaning: to challenge or resist a proposal politely
vocabulary.example: I want to push back on the timeline; two weeks is not realistic.

vocabulary.meaning: the most important or decisive point
vocabulary.example: The crux of the issue is that we never agreed on what done means.

vocabulary.meaning: transition acknowledging a point before adding a contrasting one
vocabulary.example: The design is solid. With that said, I would simplify the API.

vocabulary.meaning: to reduce the risk of a plan before committing
vocabulary.example: Let us de-risk the migration with a read-only pilot first.

vocabulary.meaning: a constraint or deadline that compels a decision or action
vocabulary.example: The conference demo is a forcing function for shipping the onboarding flow.

vocabulary.meaning: to postpone a topic (US usage); in UK usage it can mean to bring it up
vocabulary.example: Let us table the pricing discussion until we have the churn data.

vocabulary.meaning: looking back with knowledge you did not have at the time
vocabulary.example: In hindsight, we should have load-tested before the launch.

vocabulary.meaning: to commit more strongly to a course of action
vocabulary.example: After the pilot succeeded we doubled down on the enterprise segment.

vocabulary.meaning: the essential point is
vocabulary.example: It boils down to whether we trust the vendor's uptime.

vocabulary.meaning: an idea that cannot succeed or be accepted
vocabulary.example: Storing passwords in plain text is a non-starter.

vocabulary.meaning: to bring a problem to people's attention
vocabulary.example: I want to surface a risk before we commit to the date.

vocabulary.word: the long pole in the tent
vocabulary.meaning: the task that determines the total duration
vocabulary.example: Security review is the long pole in the tent for this release.

vocabulary.meaning: to share an idea informally to gather support before a formal proposal
vocabulary.example: I socialized the platform team idea with a few leads before the offsite.

vocabulary.word: to be on the same page
vocabulary.meaning: to share the same understanding
vocabulary.example: Before we estimate, let us make sure we are on the same page about scope.

vocabulary.meaning: a balance between two desirable but conflicting qualities
vocabulary.example: The tradeoff is latency versus consistency.

vocabulary.meaning: to reduce commitment or risk by keeping options open
vocabulary.example: We hedged by keeping the old pipeline running in parallel.

vocabulary.meaning: to pause and consider the bigger picture
vocabulary.example: Let me take a step back and explain why this matters.

vocabulary.meaning: to say something directly without softening
vocabulary.example: To put it bluntly, the current architecture will not survive the next customer.

vocabulary.meaning: the final result or most important consideration
vocabulary.example: The bottom line is we ship on Tuesday or we lose the pilot.

vocabulary.meaning: to return to a topic later
vocabulary.example: Let us circle back on hiring after the roadmap review.

vocabulary.meaning: an area where someone lacks awareness
vocabulary.example: Cost was a blind spot for the team until finance asked.

vocabulary.meaning: to argue convincingly in favour of
vocabulary.example: I will make the case for a platform team in the next planning cycle.

vocabulary.meaning: an obvious problem nobody wants to discuss
vocabulary.example: The elephant in the room is that the founder still approves every PR.

vocabulary.word: to err on the side of
vocabulary.meaning: to choose the safer of two options when unsure
vocabulary.example: We err on the side of over-communicating during incidents.

vocabulary.meaning: a temporary solution
vocabulary.example: The cron job is a stopgap until the queue is in place.

vocabulary.meaning: to reduce the size of a project deliberately
vocabulary.example: We scoped down the launch to three regions.

vocabulary.meaning: to embrace something fully rather than resist it
vocabulary.example: We leaned into async communication instead of fighting the time zones.

vocabulary.meaning: to increase gradually; also to get a new hire productive
vocabulary.example: New engineers ramp up in about six weeks.

vocabulary.meaning: a guiding long-term goal or metric
vocabulary.example: Weekly active teams is our north star metric.

vocabulary.meaning: to take full responsibility for a result
vocabulary.example: Whoever leads the migration owns the outcome, including the incidents.

vocabulary.meaning: invitation to imagine a scene, used to open a story
vocabulary.example: Picture this: it is 3 a.m., and the pager goes off for the fourth time.

vocabulary.meaning: to skip ahead in a story
vocabulary.example: Fast-forward to launch day, and the queue is empty.

vocabulary.meaning: I was unaware at the time, used to build suspense
vocabulary.example: Little did I know the backup had been failing for a month.

vocabulary.meaning: used to reveal a surprising fact
vocabulary.example: As it turns out, the bug was in the config, not the code.

vocabulary.meaning: the main lesson or conclusion
vocabulary.example: The takeaway is simple: test the rollback, not just the deploy.

vocabulary.meaning: for that purpose
vocabulary.example: We want faster reviews; to that end, PRs are now capped at 400 lines.

vocabulary.meaning: in the opposite way
vocabulary.example: Conversely, over-communicating can bury the signal.

vocabulary.meaning: admitting a point before countering
vocabulary.example: Granted, the rewrite is risky, but the current system is riskier.

vocabulary.meaning: to emphasize
vocabulary.example: The outage underscores why we need a status page.

vocabulary.meaning: convincing and attention-holding
vocabulary.example: The data makes a compelling case for usage-based pricing.

vocabulary.meaning: to be honest and direct, often before delivering bad news
vocabulary.example: To be candid, the demo is not ready.

vocabulary.meaning: a quick check that something is reasonable
vocabulary.example: Can you do a sanity check on these estimates?

vocabulary.meaning: to get people to agree on direction
vocabulary.example: The one-pager helped drive alignment across product and engineering.

vocabulary.meaning: to contribute an opinion
vocabulary.example: I would like security to weigh in before we pick a vendor.

vocabulary.meaning: available capacity of a person or team
vocabulary.example: We do not have the bandwidth for a second migration this quarter.

books.title: The Manager's Path
books.author: Camille Fournier
books.notes: Reading one chapter per week; explaining each aloud before moving on.
ideas: Mentoring is a skill you practise on purpose, not a personality trait.
Tech leads are the first role where your output is the team's output.
quotes: Your job is not to write code; your job is to make sure the code gets written.

books.title: Made to Stick
books.author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
books.notes: Framework for making ideas memorable: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories.
ideas: The curse of knowledge: once you know something, you cannot imagine not knowing it.
Concrete beats abstract every time in communication.
Stories are simulations that prepare people to act.
quotes: Abstraction makes it harder to understand an idea and to remember it.
To be simple, find the core of the idea.
prompts: Apply the SUCCESs checklist to your last architecture proposal.
Retell the Nordstrom story from the book and explain why it works.
